fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "From Moab Caves to a Goat Homestead", "body": "Lupine grew up in Fairfield County, Connecticut, where, as she puts it, going to live in caves or dumpster diving was not considered normal. By her late twenties she was living outside Moab, Utah, backpacking and sleeping in caves for fun out of an interest in wilderness survival. She describes first noticing a difference in her functional capabilities between the wilderness and town, recounts eventually hitting her cell phone with a rock, and traces years of freelance painting, landscaping, foraging and dumpster diving while staying as far from cell towers as she could get, before landing on a homestead with her own herd of goats."}, {"title": "Who Funds the Research, and What to Call It", "body": "On the science, Lupine argues that the first problem is that telecommunications companies do their own research, and she points listeners to independent studies on Google or PubMed rather than asking anyone to take her word for it. Chance Garton raises a Yale study in which cell phones were placed above pregnant mouse cages. Lupine also pushes back on the vocabulary itself, saying that some people in the community now take issue with the terms electrosensitive and EHS, because framing it as something affecting only a few freaks like her, in her words, draws attention away from what she believes is a far broader issue."}, {"title": "Thresholds, Alpha Levels and Risk Factors", "body": "Lupine describes what she calls the alpha levels, thresholds she says are usually crossed after one large exposure. She recounts a month of hitchhiking that included sleeping under high voltage lines and being dropped off near cell towers, capped by following a friend up a cell tower, and then a second thresholding effect years later after an episode in a hospital waiting room. She wrote in her book that ninety percent of sufferers are female, but tells Chance she is revising that view. The risk factors she associates with it include chemical sensitivity, mercury fillings, gluten intolerance, candida and black mold."}, {"title": "What Lupine Says Shielding Can and Cannot Do", "body": "Asked about solutions, Lupine is as blunt about what she thinks fails as about what she favors. She calls the shielding beanies and special magic underwear sold online a waste of money, says a suit she bought stopped working for her after a couple of wearings, and argues that partial metal shielding can bounce radiation around because it is not a closed Faraday cage. She reports mixed results with shielded bed canopies, mentions a wall coating of sand and wood glue credited in her book to her friend Gary Duncan, and Chance raises powdered shungite painted on beehives."}, {"title": "Coherence, Voltage and the Case for Solutions", "body": "In a long solo second half, Chance Garton reframes the subject around personal coherence rather than pure avoidance. Drawing on his biofield tuning practice and Eileen McKusick's book Electric Body, Electric Health, he argues that constantly tuning out background hum, fluorescent light and dissonant fields quietly drains a personal battery. He reads passages from Charles Fillmore and Phineas Quimby of the early New Thought and Christian Science movements, notes he is not endorsing those figures wholesale, and lands on his own view that a coherent field entrains a dissonant one. He says he took the episode on so the solutions, not the alarm, would carry it."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Julia Lupine is an author and goat wranglin' homesteader who spent many years as a wilderness survivalist, living with nothing but nature and the contents of her backpack. We discuss her new book, Under A Rock: An Electrosensitive Survival Guide, including topics like research on the biological effects of EMFs, the electric human body, symptoms of EMF sensitivity, clothing materials that decrease electrostatic intensity, and more.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we question if electro sensitivity can or should be cured, gaining personal energetic coherence to convert dissonant fields into livable ones, getting out of victim mentality, and a variety of other solutions including diet, herbalism, materials, and grounding techniques and technologies.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Keeping the Sense, Losing the Symptoms", "body": "Chance opens the extension with a section of Julia's book on why electrosensitivity cannot or should not be cured, arguing that sensitivity is a widened perceptual lens worth keeping even if the symptoms could be separated from it. Julia answers that, in her view, AC current barely exists in nature and overloads an innate electro sense she links to magnetite and to magnetoreception in birds. Her cyanide analogy casts the reaction as a sign of poisoning rather than a personal flaw, and she argues humans cannot adapt that fast, just as people thrown in water will not grow gills."}, {"title": "Orgonite, Crystals and Personal Coherence", "body": "Chance asks whether Julia's thinking on orgonite, shungite and crystals has shifted, recalling a man who planted orgonite at cell towers across Arizona. Julia says she respects researchers like Mitch but no longer sees orgonite as an answer for severe cases, finds quartz and shungite mildly helpful to the energy field at most, and would rather wear a thrift store leather coat than buy any pendant or harmonizer. Chance offers his own belief that syntropy, pictured as metronomes falling into sync, lets a coherent personal field entrain dissonant ones, and credits his Qigong practice with giving him a field sensitivity that is not symptomatic."}, {"title": "No Room for Victim Mentality", "body": "Chance reads the line from Julia's book that sinking into victim mentality may be more dangerous than the EMFs themselves. Julia describes going from a tough backpacker who lived in caves and in the desert to someone knocked flat by chemical smells and friends' phones, all while being told she was crazy. Her answer was to drop self pity and focus on goals, even when a trip to town becomes a chess game around smart meters, power lines and cell towers. She also champions laughter, admits she once judged people for their technology, and now urges patience with others and with yourself."}, {"title": "Grounding Tricks and Building From Scratch", "body": "Julia walks through the grounding methods she uses, from bare feet and sleeping on the ground to her friend Gary's spoon wrapped in copper lamp cord and wired to a wet copper rod in the soil. She adds hot rocks warmed on the stove, mud or bentonite clay, river plunges, Epsom salt baths and morning sun. She warns against mats plugged into a wall's ground wire, suggests a sand tray by the computer, and shows the lead glasses she is about to test. On building, she describes a backhoe dug hole for a small log sleep cabin and a friend's pallet cabin whose signal dropped to under one bar."}, {"title": "Her Herbs, Eyesight and Diet", "body": "Chance singles out yarrow, tying it to his idea that these symptoms are a problem of flow, charge and discharge. Julia explains the name Achillea millefolium, after Achilles staunching his warriors' blood, says she drinks yarrow most mornings, and lists lion's mane, cat's claw, red clover and medicinal mushrooms. She credits herbalism with giving her a research project instead of victimhood, and tells how eyebright cleared a hives problem for her. Chance links screen strain on the eyes to the sacral and third eye pairing he sees in clients, and Julia closes on her organic diet, raw goat milk and miso, and recommends The Invisible Rainbow."}]
